newsitem.title: UK: Eurotunnel to seek longer concession.
newsitem.headline: Eurotunnel to seek longer concession.

text.p: Eurotunnel SA/Plc will ask Britain and France to extend the state concession for the channel tunnel in a bid to improve the profit prospects for its shareholders, outgoing chairman Sir Alastair Morton said on Monday.
Morton said the move had been suggested by the two debt negotiators, appointed by a French court this February.
"We will now request it in the coming weeks and the answer will be forthcoming, we think, in the coming weeks," he told a news conference here. The current concession expires in 2052.
Morton said he had no prediction of the outcome, and added that a practical aim would be seek to add about 30 years.

In comments that echoed those of his French counterpart Patrick Ponsolle in Paris, Morton said the idea of extension would be to help recompense shareholders for bearing the burden of the company's debt restructuring in its first decades.

While both commented that the British government had recently agreed a 999-year concession for the builders and operators of the Channel Tunnel Rail Link for high-speed trains between Folkestone and London, Morton noted that France had never given any kind of concession for more than 99 years.
Therefore, Morton said, the expectation would be somewhere between the current 65 year life and 99 years.
A spokeswoman for Britain's Department of Transport said it was not yet possible to comment on how any application would be handled until an approach had been made by Eurotunnel.
"It would depend on what they came asking for," she said.

Morton noted that if "a significant extension" was secured it would open the way for a possible second warrant issue that has been planned as a one-for-eight issue, entitling holders to subscribe for a new share at 130p before December 2001.
The key function of these "extension warrants", if taken up by shareholders, would be to redeem equity notes otherwise issuable to the banks within the debt rejig.

They would help bolster the current shareholders' total stake in the company, and Eurotunnel calculated that if all 115 million warrants were issued and exercised, they would redeem 87 million units otherwise issuable to banks at the end of 2003.
That would serve to protect the shareholders' stake at over 50 percent of the total, and in combination with other warrants, could take their interest to 55.5 percent of the total capital.
Morton said the concept behind the idea was that, "A way should be found to give existing shareholders a larger share of the benefit of the extension -- if one is granted."
